chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Volatility Smile and Skew

lessons.title: Smile vs Skew: Naming the Shapes You See

children.text: Two Named Shapes, One Underlying Question

The last lesson explained why the IV curve is not flat. This one gives the shapes it actually takes real names, so you can describe precisely what you are looking at on any chain, in any asset class, instead of just gesturing at "the curve looks weird." There are two shapes worth knowing by name, and which one you get depends entirely on what kind of tail risk the underlying actually carries.
The Volatility Smile: Symmetric Fear on Both Sides

A volatility smile is roughly symmetric: IV is lowest at the ATM strike and rises by a similar amount as you move away from spot in either direction, up or down. Plotted out, it curves upward on both edges like a smiling mouth, hence the name. This shape shows up most classically in currency options, and USD/INR is a good example of why. A currency pair is a relative price between two economies. A sharp move can come from either side: the rupee weakening on capital outflows or a global dollar rally, or the rupee strengthening sharply on strong inflows or dollar weakness. Both tails are genuinely live possibilities, so the market prices extra premium symmetrically on both sides, not just one.

Notice the near-symmetry: IV at 3% below spot (8.2%) and 3% above spot (8.0%) land close together, both well above the 6.5% ATM figure. Neither side dominates the way it does on an equity index. That is the fingerprint of a smile.
The Volatility Skew (or Smirk): Equity's One-Sided Fear

The Nifty chart from the last two lessons is the other canonical shape: IV highest at the low, put-side strikes, declining fairly steadily through the ATM strike, and lowest at the high, call-side strikes. This is usually called a volatility skew, and you will also hear it called a volatility smirk, particularly in equity index markets. The two words get used loosely and often interchangeably, but the more precise distinction is this: "skew" describes the overall downward tilt of the curve, while "smirk" specifically refers to a skew that is not perfectly straight, one where even the deepest OTM calls show a slight upward curl of their own, a faint echo of a smile layered on top of the dominant downward tilt. Real equity index curves are almost always smirks in this precise sense, even though everyone, including this course, calls them skew for short.
Not Just Equities: A Quick Look at Other Shapes

Equity indices are not the only shape in town, and it is worth knowing the map even in a course centred on Nifty and Bank Nifty. Some commodities, crude oil being the standard example, often show the tilt running the other way: higher IV on the call side than the put side. A sudden supply shock, a geopolitical flashpoint or an unexpected OPEC decision, can spike prices sharply upward far more suddenly than crude typically grinds lower, so the market prices more premium into upside protection. Individual stocks can land almost anywhere on this spectrum depending on their own specific risk: a stock that is a live takeover target, for instance, often skews the other way from the broader index, since the dominant uncertain scenario is a sudden upward jump on deal news, not a crash.

body.caption: Three IV curve shapes and where you actually see them

cells: Roughly symmetric U-shape; lowest at ATM, rises similarly on both sides
Either side of a currency pair can spike; tail risk is genuinely two-sided
Downward-sloping; highest at low (put) strikes, lowest at high (call) strikes
Equity indices: Nifty, Bank Nifty, and most major global indices since 1987
Crashophobia: a persistent, one-sided premium for downside crash protection
Upward-sloping; higher IV at high (call) strikes than low (put) strikes
Some commodities (e.g. crude oil), and single stocks facing takeover or deal risk
Sudden supply shocks or deal news can spike prices sharply upward

children.text: Reading the Shape: Strike vs Delta

Every chart in this lesson plots IV against strike price, the way a retail option chain does, which is intuitive but has a limit: a Nifty strike 400 points from spot and a ₹640 stock's strike ₹15 from spot are not comparable distances at all. Desks instead often plot IV against delta or

, which measures distance from ATM in relative, percentage, or probability terms rather than raw price points. Plotted that way, a Nifty skew and a stock's skew become genuinely comparable shapes side by side, regardless of how differently priced the two underlyings are. Strike-based charts are the right place to start, since they match exactly what you see on a live chain; delta-based charts are what you will move toward once Chapter 4 gets into comparing and building full surfaces.

markDefs.definition: How far a strike sits from being at-the-money, expressed in relative terms (percentage distance from spot, or via the option's delta) rather than in raw price points. Two strikes on different underlyings can have the same moneyness even if their price distance from spot looks completely different.

body.text: A strike 400 points away from a 24,800 Nifty spot is about 1.6% out of the money. The same 1.6% moneyness on a ₹640 stock is only about ₹10 away from spot. Comparing "400 points" to "₹10" tells you nothing; comparing "1.6% OTM" to "1.6% OTM" tells you exactly how their skews stack up.

body.title: Predicting a shape from the story
body.question: You pull up the option chain for a stock that just became a live takeover target. The dominant uncertainty is whether a formal acquisition offer arrives, pushing the price up sharply, or falls through, leaving the price roughly where it is. Which shape would you expect its IV curve to lean toward?
options: A steep equity-index-style skew: high put IV, low call IV, exactly like Nifty typically shows
A lean toward higher call-side IV relative to put-side IV, since the dominant uncertain scenario here is a sharp upward jump on deal news, not a crash
A perfectly flat curve, since individual stocks never show any skew
It is impossible for a single stock's shape to differ from the index it belongs to
body.explanation: The skew a stock shows follows the specific tail risk the market is actually worried about for that stock, not a fixed rule. A takeover target's real uncertainty sits on the upside (deal announced or not), so its call-side IV tends to run relatively richer than the broad market's usual downside-heavy skew, even though the same stock might show an ordinary equity-style skew before the takeover story existed.

body.title: Farhan's strangle assumption
body.scenario: Farhan wants to sell a Nifty weekly strangle: a call 400 points above spot and a put 400 points below spot, the same distance on both sides. He expects the index to stay range-bound and assumes both legs will hand him roughly equal premium, since they are "equally far" from spot.
body.prompt: Using what you know about the equity skew, explain why Farhan's two legs will not actually collect equal premium, and which side carries more risk relative to what he is paid for it.
body.modelAnswer: Because Nifty carries a downward-sloping skew, the put strike 400 points below spot sits at a meaningfully higher IV than the call strike 400 points above spot, even though the two are the same distance away in price. A higher IV means a richer premium, so Farhan will actually collect more rupees on the put leg than on the call leg, not the equal split he assumed. This is not a free bonus. The put leg is richer priced precisely because it sits on the side of the market that carries genuine crash risk, the exact fear that has been priced into equity skew since 1987. Farhan is being paid more for that leg because he is taking on more of the tail risk that matters, not because the market made a pricing mistake in his favor.

columns.label: Volatility Smile
points: Roughly symmetric U-shape around the ATM strike
Classic example: currency pairs such as USD/INR
Lowest IV sits right at the money on both charts and desks

columns.label: Volatility Skew / Smirk
points: Downward-sloping, with a faint upward curl at the deepest OTM calls (the "smirk")
Classic example: equity indices such as Nifty and Bank Nifty
Reflects crashophobia: one-sided, persistent downside protection demand
Can invert into an upward skew for underlyings with dominant upside risk (some commodities, takeover targets)

body.text: The shape of an IV curve is not decoration, it is a direct readout of which tail the market is actually worried about. Symmetric fear draws a smile. One-sided fear draws a skew. The direction the curve tilts tells you exactly where the market thinks the real danger sits.

points: A volatility smile is roughly symmetric around the ATM strike, most classically seen in currency options like USD/INR, since both sides of a currency pair carry genuine tail risk.
A volatility skew (often more precisely a smirk) slopes downward from low strikes to high strikes, the standard shape for equity indices like Nifty and Bank Nifty since 1987.
"Skew" describes the overall downward tilt; "smirk" more precisely describes a skew with a slight upward curl at the deepest OTM calls, which is what real equity index curves usually look like.
Not every underlying skews the same direction: some commodities and stocks with dominant upside risk (takeover targets, deal speculation) can show the opposite, upward-tilted shape.
Plotting IV against delta or moneyness, rather than raw strike price, is what lets you compare skew shapes fairly across underlyings priced very differently.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. The USD/INR smile figures and the Farhan scenario are hypothetical and illustrative, not live market data. Always check live prices and IV on NSE, your broker's terminal, or your currency derivatives platform before trading, and consult a SEBI-registered advisor for personalised advice.
